Detect an injected effect of known size

Source: R/power.R
cpspwr.Rd

Adds an effect of each given size to the data, reruns the whole detection procedure, and reports how often it was found. The result is a power curve, and the smallest size detected reliably is the smallest effect the analysis could have seen. Use it before reporting a null result, to show whether the analysis could have found an effect of the size that matters.

Usage

cpspwr(
  data,
  stat,
  inject,
  sizes = c(0, 0.2, 0.5),
  trt = NULL,
  n = 99L,
  reps = 10L,
  alpha = 0.05,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

stat

A function of one data frame returning a single finite number (for example a correlation or a difference in means).

inject

A function of (data, size) returning the data with an effect of that size added. It is the caller's, because what counts as an effect of size 0.2 is a modelling decision and not something this function can guess.

sizes

Numeric vector of effect sizes to try (default c(0, 0.2, 0.5)). 0 is added if absent, since the detection rate there is the false-positive rate and belongs on the same curve. Duplicates are removed and the sizes sorted.

trt

Name of the column permuted to build the null, as in cpsfals(). Required.

n

Permutations per test, a whole number of at least 9 (default 99).

reps

Repetitions per size, a whole number of at least 1 (default 10). The detection rate at each size is out of this many, so its resolution is 1 / reps.

alpha

Significance threshold for counting a detection (default 0.05).

seed

Optional integer seed; NULL (the default) uses the session's random number state.

Value

A list of class c("bricklayer_power", "list"):

curve

data frame with one row per size: size, detected (integer), reps (integer, the usable repetitions) and rate (detected / reps, NA when none was usable).

alpha, n, reps, treatment

the settings used.

smadet

the smallest positive size found at a rate of at least 0.8, or NA when no size reached it.

false_positive_rate

the rate at size 0.

Details

This is the positive control that cpsfals() lacks: its four are all negative. Those establish that the finding is not an artefact; this establishes that a real effect would not have been missed. A study that passes every falsification control and has no power against the effect it was looking for has not found that the effect is absent – it has found nothing either way, and the two are routinely reported as the same thing.

For each size (0 is always added) and each of reps repetitions, the statistic is computed on the data passed through the injector, as inject(data, size), and a permutation null is built by shuffling the trt column n times and recomputing the statistic. The two-sided permutation p-value is $$p = \frac{1 + \#\{|T^*| \ge |T|\}}{1 + n_{ok}}$$ over the \(n_{ok}\) permutations with a finite statistic (Phipson and Smyth's correction, so \(p\) is never 0), and the effect counts as detected when \(p \le \alpha\). A repetition whose injection or observed statistic fails (error or non-finite value) is skipped and not counted in reps. Since the data are the same in every repetition, inject should add randomness of its own (new noise, a resampled effect) when repetitions are meant to differ; otherwise only the permutations vary.

The cost is \(|sizes| \times reps \times (n + 1)\) evaluations of stat. A progress bar is drawn on stderr unless options(morie.quiet = TRUE). With seed, R's random number state is set for the run and restored afterwards; without it, the run uses and advances the session's generator.

Errors: data not a data frame of at least 4 rows; stat or inject not a function; trt missing or not a column; n below 9; reps below 1; n so small that \(1/(n+1) > \alpha\), so that nothing could ever be detected.

See also

cpsfals() for the negative controls.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(120), y = rnorm(120))
# inject a linear effect of x on y
inj <- function(z, size) {
  z$y <- z$y + size * z$x
  z
}
pw <- cpspwr(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj,
                    sizes = c(0, 0.3, 0.6), trt = "x",
                    n = 99, reps = 5, seed = 42)
pw$curve
#>   size detected reps rate
#> 1  0.0        0    5    0
#> 2  0.3        5    5    1
#> 3  0.6        5    5    1
pw
#> ── Positive controls: an injected effect of known size ───────────
#>   99 permutations, 5 repetition(s) per size, alpha 0.05
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   size 0          detected  0/5   rate 0.00
#>   size 0.3        detected  5/5   rate 1.00
#>   size 0.6        detected  5/5   rate 1.00
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   smallest size detected at a rate of 0.8: 0.3
#>   a null result is informative only about effects at least this
#>   large; smaller ones would have been missed
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# The rate at size 0 estimates the false-positive rate. With few
# repetitions it is usually 0, because alpha is small -- five draws
# at 0.05 come up empty about three times in four -- so read it as a
# sanity check that it is not LARGE, not as an estimate of alpha.
pw$curve[pw$curve$size == 0, "rate"]
#> [1] 0

# an injection with fresh noise each time, and effects too small to be
# detected in four repetitions: the smallest detected size is NA
inj2 <- function(z, size) {
  z$y <- z$y + size * z$x + stats::rnorm(nrow(z), sd = 0.5)
  z
}
cpspwr(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj2, sizes = c(0.1, 0.2),
              trt = "x", n = 49, reps = 4, seed = 7)$smadet
#> [1] NA

# too few permutations to ever reach alpha = 0.05
try(cpspwr(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj, trt = "x", n = 9))
#> Error : with 9 permutations the smallest p-value is 0.1, which is above alpha = 0.05: no size could ever be detected
